docs.title: pgdispatch
docs.text:
Reliable webhook delivery for Python apps. It needs only the PostgreSQL you already have.

You publish an event in the same transaction as your business change. pgdispatch then delivers it to every subscribed endpoint. Each request is signed according to Standard Webhooks. Failed requests are retried, a circuit breaker protects endpoints that are down, and every attempt is logged.

async with session.begin():
    order.status = "paid"
    await webhooks.publish(session, "order.paid", {"id": order.id})
  • Nothing new to run. The queue, the retry schedule and the attempt log are tables in your database.
  • No lost events. The outbox is transactional, delivery is at-least-once, and workers can be killed at any time.
  • Webhooks are the main feature. You get signatures, secret rotation, a circuit breaker, ordering, replay and multi-tenancy.
  • Works with FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2.0, Django and asyncpg.

Get started Concepts

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
┌──────────── your application ────────────┐
            │  publish()   endpoints.*   deliveries.*   │
            └─────┬────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                  │ same tx        │ management
                  ▼                ▼
   ┌──────────────── PostgreSQL: schema "pgdispatch" ─────────────────┐
   │ endpoints   events   deliveries (the queue)   attempts   workers │
   └──────┬──────────────────────▲──────────────────────▲─────────────┘
   NOTIFY │              claim   │ SKIP LOCKED          │ results (batched)
          ▼                      │                      │
   ┌───────────────────── worker (N processes) ──────────────────────┐
   │ dispatch loop ──▶ send tasks (aiohttp, signed) ──▶ recorder     │
   │ maintenance: heartbeat · metrics · LISTEN health · clean-up     │
   └──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                                  ▼ HTTPS
                          customer endpoints

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
Table Holds Notes endpoints URL, event_types[], secrets (jsonb, newest first), headers, rate limit, circuit breaker state GIN index on event_types for fan-out events id (UUIDv7, time-ordered), type, owner, payload jsonb, idempotency key unique partial index on the idempotency key deliveries event × endpoint, status, attempt_count, next_attempt_at, locked_until partial index on next_attempt_at for the hot claim query attempts one row per HTTP request: status, body (≤ 4 KB), duration, error written in bulk workers live workers and their heartbeats used for status and rate-limit sharing schema_migrations applied migration versions

Fan-out at publish time. publish() inserts the deliveries right away, so the subscriptions are fixed at the moment of the event, and workers only read one table. It finds subscribers with one array-overlap test (event_types && candidates). The candidates are every pattern that can match the type: ["*", "a.b.c", "a.*", "a.b.*"]. This works because wildcards are only allowed as a trailing segment.

docs.title: The worker
docs.text:
• Dispatch waits for LISTEN notifications, a finished batch or the polling interval. It then claims up to the number of free slots. Claiming also moves endpoints whose cool-down has ended to half-open, and claims exactly one probe for each of them. A per-endpoint limit is applied inside the claim query with a window function, so a slow endpoint cannot take every slot.
  • Send tasks apply the endpoint's rate limit (an in-memory GCRA bucket, shared between live workers), sign the body once, POST it and classify the answer.
  • Recorder collects results and writes them in a single transaction per batch: it locks the deliveries in id order, applies the updates with attempt_count fencing, bulk-inserts the attempts and updates the circuit breakers. Endpoints that are healthy and only saw successes are not touched, so a busy endpoint never becomes a lock hotspot. A send task gives up its slot only after its result is stored, so the next claim always sees the current breaker and ordering state.
  • Maintenance sends heartbeats, refreshes metrics, re-establishes LISTEN if its connection drops, and runs the retention clean-up under an advisory lock.

docs.title: One SQL path for every framework
docs.text:
The same operations run on asyncpg, SQLAlchemy (any async driver) and Django (psycopg, synchronously). Each operation is written once, as a generator that yields queries and receives rows:

def get_endpoint(endpoint_id: UUID, *, owner_id: OwnerFilter) -> Operation[Endpoint]:
    rows = yield Query("SELECT ... WHERE e.id = CAST(:id AS uuid) ...", {"id": str(endpoint_id)})
    return Endpoint.from_row(first_or_not_found(rows, "endpoint", endpoint_id))

run_async and run_sync drive the generator against an executor for the driver in use. Executors only translate placeholders and run one statement, so the business logic stays in one place. The worker is asyncpg-only and uses array parameters (unnest) for its batched statements.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
• Leases instead of long transactions. Holding a row lock during an HTTP request would tie up connections and make crashes costly. Leases make every worker disposable.
  • aiohttp for outbound HTTP. Its connection pool scales to hundreds of concurrent requests per process, and its resolver hook is the public API that lets the SSRF filter connect to the IP it checked.
  • Signing is built in. HMAC over three headers is a few lines of standard library code. The test suite checks it against the reference standardwebhooks package, which removes a dependency without losing compatibility.
  • No ORM models for pgdispatch tables. The schema is owned by versioned SQL migrations, shared by the CLI, Alembic and Django. Two sources of truth would drift apart.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and the project uses Semantic Versioning.
The first public release.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Transactional outbox: Webhooks.publish() joins the caller's transaction (asyncpg, SQLAlchemy 2.0 async, Django).
  • Fan-out to subscribed endpoints with *, exact and prefix.* patterns, isolated by owner_id.
  • Idempotent publishing (idempotency_key) and ordered delivery (ordering_key).
  • Delivery worker: claiming with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and leases, LISTEN/NOTIFY wake-ups, batched result recording, per-endpoint concurrency limits and rate limits, graceful shutdown.
  • Standard Webhooks signatures; secret rotation with a grace period; optional Fernet encryption of secrets at rest.
  • Retry schedule with jitter and Retry-After; per-endpoint circuit breaker; automatic disabling of endpoints that keep failing; 410 Gone handling.
  • SSRF protection: URL validation, a resolver that pins connections to checked public addresses, no redirects.
  • Management API for endpoints, deliveries (list, attempts, retry, cancel) and events (list, replay); test events.
  • FastAPI router for customer-facing endpoint management; ASGI lifespan integration.
  • Django app with migrations, a synchronous facade and the pgdispatch_worker command; an Alembic helper.
  • pgdispatch CLI: migrate, worker, status, deliveries, retry, replay, endpoints, cleanup.
  • Prometheus metrics, a Grafana dashboard, alert rules, structured logs and hooks.
  • Retention clean-up of old events, deliveries and attempts.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The whole model has five entities. An event creates one delivery for each subscribed endpoint. Each delivery makes one or more attempts.

Entity What it is Example Event An immutable fact with a type and a JSON payload order.paid, {"id": 42} Endpoint A receiver URL with its own signing secret and settings https://shop.example.com/hooks Subscription The event types an endpoint wants (event_types) ["order.*", "refund.created"] Delivery The task "deliver event X to endpoint Y", with a status pending → succeeded Attempt One HTTP request of a delivery, with its response attempt 3, 503, 1,200 ms

docs.title: Event types and subscriptions
docs.text:
An event type is a dot-separated name made of letters, digits, _ and -, for example order.paid or invoice.payment_failed. An endpoint subscribes with patterns:

Pattern Matches * every event order.paid exactly order.paid order.* order.paid, order.refund.created, … (but not order itself)

Subscriptions are resolved when the event is published. An endpoint created later does not receive older events. You can replay them to it.

docs.title: Owners (tenants)
docs.text:
Every endpoint and event can have an owner_id, for example a merchant or organisation id. An event is delivered only to endpoints with the same owner. Events without an owner go only to endpoints without an owner. This keeps one customer's data from reaching another customer's endpoint.

Management methods take owner_id too. When you pass it, the call is limited to that owner, and objects of other owners behave as if they don't exist. This is how the FastAPI router isolates tenants. If you leave owner_id out (internal, trusted code), the call works across all owners. owner_id=None means "objects without an owner".

docs.title: Delivery lifecycle
docs.text:
┌───────── retry (5 s … 10 h) ─────────┐
          ▼                                      │
 ──▶ pending ──claim──▶ in_flight ──2xx──▶ succeeded
                            │
                            ├──error, attempts left──▶ pending
                            ├──error, no attempts left──▶ failed
                            └──410 Gone──▶ cancelled (endpoint disabled)
Status Meaning pending Waiting for its next attempt (next_attempt_at). in_flight A worker has claimed it and is sending it. The claim is a lease that expires if the worker dies. succeeded The endpoint answered with a 2xx status. failed Every attempt in the retry schedule failed. You can retry or replay it at any time. cancelled Abandoned: the endpoint answered 410 Gone, or the delivery was cancelled manually.

docs.title: What counts as success
docs.text:
Response Result 2xx Success. 410 Gone The receiver asks to unsubscribe: the endpoint is disabled and the delivery cancelled. 429, 5xx, timeout, connection or DNS error Retried on schedule. Retry-After is respected for 429 and 503. 3xx Treated as an error. Redirects are never followed (SSRF protection). Any other 4xx Retried. The receiver may have broken its server only for a while.

Every failure counts towards the endpoint's circuit breaker.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
By default deliveries run in parallel and may arrive in any order. That gives the best throughput. When order matters, pass an ordering_key:

await webhooks.publish(session, "order.updated", payload, ordering_key=f"order:{order.id}")

For each endpoint, a delivery with a key is sent only after every earlier delivery with the same key has finished, whether it succeeded or failed. The cost is head-of-line blocking: an event stuck in retries holds back later events with the same key, but nothing else.

docs.title: Idempotent publishing
docs.text:
await webhooks.publish(session, "order.paid", payload, idempotency_key=f"order.paid:{order.id}")

When you publish with a key that already exists, nothing is created and you get back the original event id (result.duplicate is True). Keys are remembered for as long as events are kept (retention_days).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All settings live in one immutable WebhooksConfig. Every value can be set:

  • in code: WebhooksConfig(concurrency=100);
  • through environment variables with the PGDISPATCH_ prefix, for example PGDISPATCH_CONCURRENCY=100;
  • in Django: settings.PGDISPATCH = {"concurrency": 100}.

Arguments take priority over the environment. Durations accept a timedelta, a number of seconds (30, 0.5), a short form (250ms, 30s, 5m, 1h30m, 14d) or ISO 8601 (PT5M). The defaults are meant for production.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Setting Default Meaning db_schema pgdispatch Schema that holds the tables. retention_days 14 Events, deliveries and attempts older than this are deleted. cleanup_interval 10 min How often a worker cleans up. cleanup_batch_size 5000 Rows deleted per transaction. max_payload_bytes 256 KB Largest serialized payload accepted by publish().

docs.title: Worker
docs.text: Setting Default Meaning concurrency 50 HTTP requests in flight per worker. endpoint_concurrency 10 Requests in flight per worker to a single endpoint. batch_size 100 Deliveries claimed per query. poll_interval 1 s How often to poll, in case a NOTIFY is missed. lease_duration 30 s How long a claimed delivery stays reserved. Must be longer than request_timeout. heartbeat_interval 5 s Worker heartbeat. shutdown_timeout 25 s Grace period for requests in flight on shutdown.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text: Setting Default Meaning request_timeout 15 s Total time allowed for one request. user_agent pgdispatch/<version> User-Agent header. store_response_body true Keep receivers' response bodies in the attempt log. max_response_body_bytes 4096 How much of each response body to read and keep. outbound_proxy — Send every request through this HTTP proxy.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning retry_schedule 0, 5s, 5m, 30m, 2h, 5h, 10h, 10h The delay before each attempt. Its length is the maximum number of attempts. retry_jitter 0.2 Random spread of ±20% on each delay.

exponential_backoff() builds a schedule for you:

from datetime import timedelta
from pgdispatch import WebhooksConfig, exponential_backoff

WebhooksConfig(retry_schedule=exponential_backoff(12, initial=timedelta(seconds=10)))

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text: Setting Default Meaning failure_threshold 10 Failures in a row before the breaker opens. circuit_cooldown 5 min First pause before a probe. It doubles after each failed probe… circuit_max_cooldown 1 h …up to this limit. auto_disable_after 5 days Disable an endpoint that has failed without a break for this long. None turns this off.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning allow_http false Accept http:// endpoints. Use it in development only. allow_private_ips false Turn off SSRF protection. Use it in tests only. secret_encryption_keys — Fernet keys that encrypt signing secrets at rest. The first key encrypts, and all keys decrypt.

In the environment, set lists as JSON: PGDISPATCH_RETRY_SCHEDULE='[0, "30s", "5m"]', PGDISPATCH_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEYS='["key1", "key2"]'.

docs.title: Managing endpoints
docs.text: All examples use the async API. The Django facade (pgdispatch.django.webhooks) has the same methods, only blocking.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
endpoint = await webhooks.endpoints.create(
    "https://merchant.example.com/webhooks",
    event_types=["order.*"],  # default: ["*"]
    owner_id="merchant_42",
    description="Production",
    headers={"X-Api-Key": "..."},  # sent with every request
    rate_limit_rps=20,  # optional per-endpoint rate limit
)
endpoint.secret  # "whsec_..." — show it to the customer once

The URL must use https and must not contain credentials or point to a private address (see Security). Custom headers cannot override webhook-*, content-type, user-agent and other headers that pgdispatch sets.

docs.title: Read, update, delete
docs.text:
await webhooks.endpoints.get(endpoint_id, owner_id="merchant_42")
await webhooks.endpoints.list(owner_id="merchant_42", enabled=True, limit=100, after=last_id)
await webhooks.endpoints.update(endpoint_id, event_types=["order.*", "refund.*"], description=None)
await webhooks.endpoints.delete(endpoint_id)  # also deletes its deliveries and attempts

update changes only the fields you pass. Pass None to clear description or rate_limit_rps.

docs.title: Enable and disable
docs.text:
await webhooks.endpoints.disable(endpoint_id, reason="customer request")
await webhooks.endpoints.enable(endpoint_id)  # also resets the circuit breaker

Pending deliveries of a disabled endpoint stay in the queue and resume when it is enabled again. New events are not fanned out to disabled endpoints.

docs.title: Signing secrets
docs.text:
secret = await webhooks.endpoints.get_secret(endpoint_id)
rotated = await webhooks.endpoints.rotate_secret(endpoint_id, grace_period=timedelta(hours=24))
rotated.secret  # the new secret

During the grace period every request carries two signatures, one per secret. The receiver can switch to the new secret whenever it is ready, and no request fails verification. Use grace_period=timedelta(0) to revoke a leaked secret immediately.

docs.title: Test events
docs.text:
await webhooks.endpoints.send_test(endpoint_id)

This sends a webhook.test event to this endpoint only, whatever it is subscribed to. It is handy for a "Send test event" button.

docs.title: Inspecting and retrying deliveries
docs.text:
failed = await webhooks.deliveries.list(endpoint_id=endpoint_id, status="failed", limit=50)
attempts = await webhooks.deliveries.attempts(failed[0].id)  # requests and responses
await webhooks.deliveries.retry(failed[0].id)  # now, with a fresh retry schedule
await webhooks.deliveries.retry_all(endpoint_id=endpoint_id)  # every failed delivery
await webhooks.deliveries.cancel(delivery_id)  # give up on a pending delivery

Lists return the newest items first. To get the next page, pass the last id as before.

docs.title: Replaying events
docs.text:
await webhooks.events.replay(event_id)  # to every endpoint subscribed now
await webhooks.events.replay(event_id, endpoint_id=endpoint_id)  # to one endpoint

Replay creates new deliveries for an existing event. Use it to backfill a newly created endpoint, or to resend after the customer fixed their server. Replays keep the original webhook-id and ignore ordering_key. An event can be replayed only to endpoints of its own owner.

docs.title: A ready-made API for your customers
docs.text:
pgdispatch.fastapi.router gives your product a complete endpoint-management API:

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from pgdispatch.fastapi import router


async def current_merchant(user=Depends(current_user)) -> str:
    return user.merchant_id


app.include_router(router(webhooks, owner=current_merchant), prefix="/webhooks")
Method Path GET /endpoints list POST /endpoints create (the response includes the secret) GET, PATCH, DELETE /endpoints/{id} read, update, delete POST /endpoints/{id}/enable, /disable GET /endpoints/{id}/secret reveal the secret POST /endpoints/{id}/rotate-secret {"grace_period_seconds": 86400} POST /endpoints/{id}/test send webhook.test GET /deliveries?endpoint_id=&status=&before= list GET /deliveries/{id} detail with attempts POST /deliveries/{id}/retry

The owner dependency is required. It authenticates the request and limits every operation to that owner.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
SQLAlchemy / FastAPIDjangoasyncpg 
pip install "pgdispatch[sqlalchemy,fastapi]"

pip install "pgdispatch[django]"

pip install pgdispatch

You need Python 3.10 or newer and PostgreSQL 13 or newer. With Django, the PostgreSQL version must also be one your Django release supports (Django 5.x needs 14+, Django 6 needs 15+). The optional encryption extra adds encryption of signing secrets at rest (see Security).

docs.title: 1. Create the schema
docs.text:
pgdispatch keeps its tables in a separate pgdispatch schema, so they never mix with yours. Choose whichever way fits your project:

pgdispatch migrate --dsn postgresql://app:secret@localhost/app

await webhooks.migrate()  # from code, e.g. on start-up
app = FastAPI(lifespan=webhooks.lifespan(migrate=True))
  • Django: add "pgdispatch.django" to INSTALLED_APPS and run python manage.py migrate.
  • Alembic: add pgdispatch to your own migration chain:
from alembic import op
from pgdispatch.sqlalchemy import run_migrations


def upgrade() -> None:
    run_migrations(op.get_bind())

Migrations are idempotent, and an advisory lock protects them, so several processes can run them at the same time without harm.

docs.title: 2. Create a Webhooks instance
docs.text:
from pgdispatch import Webhooks, WebhooksConfig
from pgdispatch.sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyBackend

webhooks = Webhooks(SQLAlchemyBackend(engine), WebhooksConfig(concurrency=50))

With plain asyncpg, use AsyncpgBackend("postgresql://..."). With Django, import the ready-made instance with from pgdispatch.django import webhooks. It is configured from settings.PGDISPATCH.

docs.title: 3. Register an endpoint
docs.text:
endpoint = await webhooks.endpoints.create(
    "https://merchant.example.com/webhooks",
    event_types=["order.*", "refund.created"],
    owner_id="merchant_42",
)
print(endpoint.secret)  # whsec_... — give it to the receiver to verify signatures

docs.title: 4. Publish events
docs.text:
async with session.begin():
    order.status = "paid"
    await webhooks.publish(session, "order.paid", {"id": order.id}, owner_id=order.merchant_id)

docs.title: 5. Run a worker
docs.text:
The worker can run inside your web process:

app = FastAPI(lifespan=webhooks.lifespan())

It can also run as separate processes, as many as you need:

pgdispatch worker --dsn postgresql://app:secret@localhost/app
python manage.py pgdispatch_worker            # Django

That's all you need. To see how delivery behaves, read Concepts. To learn how receivers verify requests, read Receiving webhooks.

docs.title: Reliability and guarantees
docs.text:
pgdispatch promises at-least-once delivery of committed events. This page explains what that covers, and where it ends.

Guarantee Yes / No Why An event from a rolled-back transaction is never sent yes The event, its deliveries and the NOTIFY belong to your transaction. A committed event is never lost yes Delivery state lives in PostgreSQL. Claims are leases that expire when a worker dies. Exactly-once delivery no A worker can crash after the receiver answered 200 but before the result was stored. Receivers deduplicate by webhook-id. Order per ordering_key Deliveries with the same key go to an endpoint one at a time. Delivery while the receiver is down about 27 hours That is the length of the default schedule. After it, the delivery is failed and can be retried or replayed. Extra infrastructure none PostgreSQL 13+.

docs.title: How a delivery stays safe
docs.text:
1. Publish. One statement inserts the event and one delivery row for each subscribed endpoint, in your transaction.
  2. Claim. A worker runs a short transaction that picks due rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, marks them in_flight with locked_until = now() + lease_duration, increments attempt_count, and commits. No lock is held while the HTTP request runs.
  3. Send. The worker signs and sends the request.
  4. Record. The result is written in a batch. Each update is fenced by attempt_count: if the lease expired and another worker already retried the delivery, the stale result is discarded. The attempt itself is still logged.

If a worker dies at any point, the lease expires and step 2 picks the delivery up again.

docs.title: Speed versus durability
docs.text: The worker's own transactions (claims and results) run with synchronous_commit = off. If the database server crashes, the last few hundred milliseconds of worker bookkeeping can be lost. This affects only bookkeeping: a lost result means the request is sent once more, which at-least-once already allows. publish() is not affected. It runs in your transaction, with your durability settings.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
Element n of retry_schedule is the delay before attempt n + 1. With the default schedule, attempts run immediately and then after 5 s, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 5 h, 10 h and 10 h, with ±20% jitter, so that retries for many failed deliveries don't arrive all at once. A Retry-After header on 429/503 can lengthen a delay, but never beyond the longest delay in the schedule.

A manual retry (deliveries.retry) starts the schedule again from the beginning. Attempt numbers keep growing, so the log stays clear.

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text:
Each endpoint has its own breaker:

  • closed: normal operation. After failure_threshold (10) failures in a row → open.
  • open: none of the endpoint's deliveries are claimed, so they don't use up their attempts while the endpoint is down. After circuit_cooldown (5 min) → half-open.
  • half-open: one probe delivery is sent. If it succeeds → closed. If it fails → open again, with a doubled cool-down (up to circuit_max_cooldown, 1 h).

Separately, an endpoint that has failed without a break for auto_disable_after (5 days) is disabled, and your on_endpoint_disabled hook is called. You can, for example, email the customer.

docs.title: Ordering in detail
docs.text: With an ordering_key, a delivery is claimed only if no earlier delivery with the same key to the same endpoint is still pending or in_flight. "Earlier" means earlier insertion. Events published one after another, the usual case, arrive in exactly that order. If two transactions publish with the same key at the same time, the one that started inserting first counts as earlier.

docs.title: Proven by tests
docs.text:
These tests run against real PostgreSQL and real worker processes, on every supported Python version and PostgreSQL 13–17 (tests/chaos):

  • a rolled-back transaction creates 0 deliveries;
  • kill -9 of a worker with 1,000 deliveries in flight: after a restart all 1,000 arrive, and none are lost;
  • 4 worker processes deliver 10,000 events, each exactly once;
  • an endpoint outage opens the breaker, and after recovery every event arrives;
  • 1,000 events with one ordering_key, handled by two competing workers, arrive strictly in order.

docs.title: Prometheus metrics
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Meaning pgdispatch_events_published_total counter event_type Events published. pgdispatch_delivery_attempts_total counter result HTTP attempts: success, http_error, timeout, network. pgdispatch_delivery_duration_seconds histogram result Duration of attempts. pgdispatch_deliveries_failed_total counter — Deliveries that used up every attempt. pgdispatch_deliveries_pending gauge — Deliveries waiting on enabled endpoints. pgdispatch_oldest_pending_age_seconds gauge — Delivery lag: how long the most overdue delivery has waited. This is the main metric to alert on. pgdispatch_endpoints_circuit_open gauge — Enabled endpoints whose breaker is open or half-open. pgdispatch_worker_batch_size histogram — Deliveries claimed per query.

The metrics are registered in prometheus_client's default registry, so they appear on your application's existing /metrics endpoint. Standalone workers serve them with --metrics-port 9100. Endpoint ids are deliberately left out of the labels, because thousands of endpoints would create too many time series. For per-endpoint details, use the CLI or the API.

contrib/ contains:

  • grafana/dashboard.json: throughput, success ratio, latency percentiles, lag, queue size, circuit breakers;
  • prometheus/alerts.yml: alerts for a lag over 5 minutes, a failure ratio over 20% for 10 minutes, a rising number of open breakers, and pending deliveries that nothing is delivering.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
pgdispatch logs through the standard logging module, under the pgdispatch logger (pgdispatch.worker, pgdispatch.hooks). Attempt records carry structured fields in extra: event_id, delivery_id, endpoint_id, attempt, status_code and duration_ms. JSON formatters and structlog pick these up.

Level What DEBUG every successful attempt INFO failed attempts, worker start and stop, clean-up WARNING circuit breaker opened, endpoint disabled, database errors (retried)

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
@webhooks.hooks.on_endpoint_disabled
async def notify_customer(endpoint: Endpoint, reason: str) -> None:
    await mailer.send(endpoint.owner_id, f"Your webhook endpoint was disabled: {reason}")


@webhooks.hooks.on_circuit_opened
def page_on_call(endpoint: Endpoint) -> None: ...


@webhooks.hooks.on_delivery_failed
async def record(delivery: Delivery) -> None: ...

Hooks run in the worker after the change has been committed. They can be plain functions or coroutines. An exception in a hook is logged and does not affect delivery.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
pgdispatch status [--json]
pgdispatch deliveries [--status S] [--endpoint ID] [--event ID] [--owner O] [--since 1h] [--json]
pgdispatch deliveries show ID [--json]
pgdispatch retry ID | pgdispatch retry --endpoint ID [--status failed] [--since 1d]
pgdispatch replay --event ID [--endpoint ID]
pgdispatch endpoints list [--owner O] [--enabled/--no-enabled] [--json]
pgdispatch endpoints enable ID | pgdispatch endpoints disable ID [--reason TEXT]
pgdispatch cleanup [--older-than 14d]
pgdispatch migrate
pgdispatch worker [--concurrency N] [--batch-size N] [--metrics-port P]

The database comes from --dsn, PGDISPATCH_DSN or DATABASE_URL. SQLAlchemy-style URLs such as postgresql+asyncpg:// are accepted.

docs.title: Publishing events
docs.text: publish() writes the event and its deliveries inside your transaction. That is the main point of pgdispatch. If the transaction commits, the event will be delivered. If it rolls back, the event never existed.

docs.title: SQLAlchemy 2.0 (async)
docs.text:
async with session.begin():
    session.add(order)
    await session.flush()
    result = await webhooks.publish(
        session,  # an AsyncSession or AsyncConnection
        "order.created",
        {"id": order.id, "total": order.total},
        owner_id=order.merchant_id,
    )

Any async PostgreSQL driver works for publishing: asyncpg or psycopg.

docs.title: asyncpg
docs.text:
from pgdispatch import AsyncpgBackend, Webhooks

webhooks = Webhooks(AsyncpgBackend("postgresql://app:secret@localhost/app"))

async with pool.acquire() as connection, connection.transaction():
    await connection.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = $1", order_id)
    await webhooks.publish(connection, "order.paid", {"id": order_id})

docs.title: Django
docs.text:
from django.db import transaction
from pgdispatch.django import webhooks

with transaction.atomic():
    order.save()
    webhooks.publish("order.shipped", {"id": order.id}, owner_id=order.shop_id)

Inside atomic() the event joins your transaction (pgdispatch uses a savepoint). Outside it, the event is committed on its own.

docs.title: Without a business transaction
docs.text:
Pass None instead of a connection to publish in a transaction of its own:

await webhooks.publish(None, "report.ready", {"url": url})

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning event_type Dot-separated type such as order.paid (at most 255 characters). payload Any JSON-serializable value; sent as data. datetime, UUID, Decimal, Enum, dataclasses and Pydantic models are converted automatically. At most max_payload_bytes (256 KB by default). owner_id Deliver only to endpoints of this owner. ordering_key Deliver events with this key one at a time, in order (see Concepts). idempotency_key Publish at most once per key.

The result is a PublishResult(event_id, deliveries, duplicate), where deliveries is the number of endpoints the event was fanned out to.

docs.title: The request body
docs.text:
Receivers get the envelope recommended by Standard Webhooks:

{"type": "order.paid", "timestamp": "2026-11-01T10:00:00.123Z", "data": {"id": 42}}

timestamp is the time the event was published. The webhook-id header holds the event id. It is the same on every attempt and every replay.

docs.title: How fast is delivery?
docs.text: The fan-out statement queues a NOTIFY, and PostgreSQL delivers it when the transaction commits. Idle workers wake up at once, so delivery typically starts a few milliseconds after the commit. If a notification is lost (for example, the connection was down), workers still poll every poll_interval (1 s).

docs.title: Receiving webhooks
docs.text: This page is for the people who receive your webhooks: your customers. You can link to it from your own API documentation.

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
POST /webhooks HTTP/1.1
content-type: application/json
user-agent: pgdispatch/0.1.0
webhook-id: 01a1985f-e246-725c-a639-369d5fd0a21b
webhook-timestamp: 1793527200
webhook-signature: v1,K5oZfzN95Z9UVu1EsfQmfVNQhnkZ2pj9o9NDN/H/pI4=

{"type":"order.paid","timestamp":"2026-11-01T10:00:00.123Z","data":{"id":42}}
Header Meaning webhook-id Unique event id. It is the same on every retry, so use it to deduplicate. webhook-timestamp Unix time of this attempt, in seconds. webhook-signature One or more space-separated v1,<base64 signature> values. During a secret rotation there are two.

docs.title: Verifying the signature
docs.text:
The scheme is Standard Webhooks:

  1. Take the secret, remove the whsec_ prefix and base64-decode the rest. That is the HMAC key.
  2. Build the signed content "{webhook-id}.{webhook-timestamp}.{raw body}".
  3. Compute HMAC-SHA256 with the key and base64-encode the result.
  4. Compare it, in constant time, with each v1, value in webhook-signature. One match is enough.
  5. Reject the request if webhook-timestamp is more than 5 minutes away from your clock. This blocks replayed requests.

Use the raw body

Sign and compare the exact bytes you received. If you parse the JSON and serialize it again, the bytes change and the signature no longer matches.

The official Standard Webhooks libraries do all of this for you:

PythonNode.jsGo 
from standardwebhooks import Webhook

payload = Webhook(secret).verify(raw_body, headers)  # raises on failure

Or, if pgdispatch is installed:

from pgdispatch import verify_signature

verify_signature(secret, headers, raw_body)

import { Webhook } from "standardwebhooks";

const payload = new Webhook(secret).verify(rawBody, headers);

wh, _ := standardwebhooks.NewWebhook(secret)
err := wh.Verify(rawBody, r.Header)

Libraries also exist for Ruby, PHP, Java, Kotlin, C#, Rust and Elixir. See the list. If you prefer no dependencies, examples/receivers has short, complete receivers in Python, Node.js and Go.

docs.title: Receiver best practices
docs.text:
• Answer quickly. Return a 2xx status as soon as the request is verified, and do the work in the background. Requests time out after 15 seconds by default.
  • Deduplicate by webhook-id. Delivery is at-least-once, so the same event can arrive twice, for example after a network failure.
  • Don't rely on order unless the sender uses ordering keys. Use the timestamp in the body to tell which event is newer.
  • To unsubscribe, answer 410 Gone. The endpoint is then disabled, and no more requests are sent.
  • Errors are retried with growing pauses for about 27 hours. After a long run of failures the endpoint is paused or disabled. The sender can resend everything you missed.

docs.title: Request signatures
docs.text: Every request is signed with HMAC-SHA256 according to Standard Webhooks. Receivers verify both where the request came from and that it was not changed. The signature covers a timestamp, which lets receivers reject replayed requests. See Receiving webhooks.

docs.title: Signing secrets
docs.text:
• Secrets look like whsec_<base64 of 32 random bytes> and are generated with secrets.token_bytes.
  • A secret is returned only by create, rotate_secret and get_secret. It never appears in repr(), logs or metrics.
  • The worker needs the plaintext secret to sign requests, so secrets cannot be hashed. They can be encrypted at rest:
pip install "pgdispatch[encryption]"
python -c "from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())"
export PGDISPATCH_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEYS='["<key>"]'

The first key encrypts new secrets, and every key in the list can decrypt. To rotate the encryption key, put a new key first and keep the old one until every endpoint secret has been rotated. Secrets stored without encryption keep working, so you can turn encryption on at any time. You can also pass any object with encrypt/decrypt methods as Webhooks(secret_cipher=...).

  • Rotate a secret with zero downtime using rotate_secret(grace_period=...). To revoke a leaked secret at once, pass grace_period=timedelta(0).

docs.title: Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
docs.text:
Your customers choose the endpoint URLs. Without protection, a customer could point your worker at http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud credentials), http://localhost:5432 or an internal admin panel. pgdispatch defends against this at every step:

When Check Endpoint created or updated https only, no credentials in the URL, no private IP literals, no localhost/.local/.internal names. Every connection The host name is resolved, and every resulting address must be public. Private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, multicast and reserved IPv4 and IPv6 ranges are rejected, including IPv4-mapped, 6to4 and Teredo forms. Every connection The socket connects to the address that was checked. DNS is not looked up again, which closes the DNS-rebinding hole. TLS still checks the certificate for the original host name. Every response Redirects are never followed.

Blocked attempts are logged with an error starting with blocked:. Proxy settings from the environment are ignored, because they would bypass these checks. To route traffic through an egress proxy on purpose, set outbound_proxy. Address filtering then becomes the proxy's job.

For local development, allow_http=True and allow_private_ips=True turn these checks off. Never enable them in production.

docs.title: Data and retention
docs.text:
• Event payloads, response bodies (up to 4 KB) and request headers are kept for retention_days (14 by default). Older data is deleted automatically. Mention this in your privacy policy and GDPR records.
  • Set store_response_body=False if receivers may return sensitive data.
  • Values of custom endpoint headers, such as API keys, are replaced with [redacted] in the attempt log.
  • Payloads are not encrypted at rest. Leave secrets out of them, or encrypt the database storage.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Please report vulnerabilities privately, as described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Running workers
docs.text: A worker claims due deliveries, sends them, and writes the results back. All coordination happens through PostgreSQL, so you can run any number of workers in any number of processes and hosts.

docs.title: In the application process
docs.text:
The simplest setup suits small and medium traffic:

app = FastAPI(lifespan=webhooks.lifespan())  # FastAPI / Starlette

async with webhooks.running_worker():  # any asyncio program
    await serve_forever()

If you already have a lifespan, nest the worker inside it:

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    async with engine.begin() as connection:
        ...
    async with webhooks.running_worker():
        yield

Several web processes

Each process with an in-app worker is one more worker. That is safe, but with many web replicas it is usually cleaner to run dedicated workers.

docs.title: As separate processes
docs.text:
pgdispatch worker --dsn postgresql://app:secret@db/app --concurrency 100 --metrics-port 9100
python manage.py pgdispatch_worker --concurrency 100 --metrics-port 9100   # Django

All PGDISPATCH_* environment variables apply (see Configuration). In Kubernetes, run workers as a Deployment and scale the replica count.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
Setting Default Notes concurrency 50 HTTP requests in flight per worker. Most of the time is spent waiting for receivers, so values of 100–500 are fine. endpoint_concurrency 10 Requests in flight per worker to one endpoint. It keeps one slow endpoint from taking every slot. batch_size 100 Deliveries claimed per query.

A worker keeps at most 5 database connections, one of which is used for LISTEN. The worker needs a direct (or session-pooled) connection: LISTEN does not work through PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode. If you use transaction pooling, workers still work by polling every poll_interval.

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
On SIGTERM or SIGINT, the worker:

  1. stops claiming new deliveries;
  2. waits up to shutdown_timeout (25 s) for requests in flight;
  3. returns deliveries that are still unfinished to pending, without counting an attempt;
  4. writes all results and removes itself from the workers table.

Set your orchestrator's grace period a little longer than shutdown_timeout. Kubernetes defaults to 30 s, which fits the default 25 s.

docs.title: Crashes
docs.text: If a worker is killed without warning (OOM, kill -9, a lost node), its claims are leases that expire after lease_duration (30 s). Another worker then picks those deliveries up. Nothing is lost, but a request that was in flight may be sent again. This is why receivers deduplicate by webhook-id.

docs.title: Housekeeping
docs.text:
Workers also:

  • send a heartbeat every heartbeat_interval. pgdispatch status shows live workers, and per-endpoint rate limits are split between them;
  • refresh the queue gauges for Prometheus;
  • delete events older than retention_days, together with their deliveries and attempts, in batches. Only one worker cleans up at a time, guarded by an advisory lock.
